screens.body:
User research is finding out what people actually need BEFORE you design. It sounds obvious, but most bad software was built by smart people solving a problem nobody had — or solving the right problem the wrong way.

Research replaces assumptions with evidence. "I think users want dark mode" is an assumption. "7 of 9 interviewees squint at the white screen on night shifts" is evidence. Design from evidence.

options: Learning what users truly need before designing, with evidence not guesses
check.question: User research is…

screens.heading: Evidence, not assumptions

screens.body:
Needs analysis maps the user's CURRENT state: what are they trying to do today, how do they do it, and where does it hurt? You're drawing the "before" picture — the messy reality your design will improve.

Example: "Braiders take bookings over DMs, lose track in long chats, and double-book Saturdays." That's a current state. Every pain point in it is a design opportunity waiting for a requirement.

options: Mapping what users do today and where it hurts — the "before" picture
check.question: Needs analysis maps…

screens.heading: Start with the "before"
screens.keyPoint: Today's pain points are tomorrow's features.

screens.body:
The best research tool is a conversation: user interviews. Ask open questions ("tell me about the last time you…"), watch them do the task in their real environment, and follow the interesting threads. Five deep interviews beat fifty shallow surveys.

Golden rules: no leading questions ("you'd love auto-reminders, right?" is a trap), more listening than talking, and watch behavior over words — what people DO contradicts what they SAY, and the doing is usually the truth.

options: Open questions, watching real behavior, no leading
Telling users your solution and asking if they like it
check.question: Good user interviews use…

screens.heading: Talk to humans
screens.keyPoint: Watch what they do, not just what they say.

screens.body:
A persona is a fictional character built from REAL research — a stand-in for a user group. "Amara, 21, SAIT student, books braids between classes, hates phone calls, pays with e-transfer." Goals, frustrations, context — one page.

Personas keep the team honest. In every design argument, someone can ask: "would Amara understand this screen?" It turns abstract "users" into a person you can empathize with — and stops design-by-opinion.

options: A research-based fictional stand-in for a user group
check.question: A persona is…

screens.heading: Meet your persona

screens.body:
Research findings become design requirements: "users lose DMs → the system must keep a booking history." This is elicitation again — but now the raw material is observations and quotes, not just interviews.

The chain is: evidence → insight → requirement. "3 of 5 braiders double-booked" (evidence) → "booking conflicts are the top pain" (insight) → "the system must warn about overlapping appointments" (requirement). Show your work; it defends your design later.
screens.heading: From findings to requirements
screens.keyPoint: Show the chain: evidence, insight, requirement.

screens.body:
Interviews are one tool among several. Surveys reach many people fast (but stay shallow). Observation — watching someone work without interrupting — reveals the workarounds people don't even notice anymore. Analytics show what thousands do, but never WHY.

Mix methods like you'd mix ingredients: interviews for depth, surveys for breadth, observation for truth, analytics for scale. Each covers the others' blind spots.

options: Interviews, surveys, observation, analytics — mixed to cover blind spots
check.question: Research methods include…

screens.heading: A full toolkit

screens.body:
Before designing the "to-be," write down the "as-is": the user's current state, step by step, with the pain points marked. This becomes your baseline — the thing your design must measurably improve.

It also keeps you humble. If the current way takes 2 minutes and your shiny design takes 5, the design lost — no matter how beautiful it is. The as-is is the score to beat.

options: The user's current workflow, documented as the baseline your design must beat
check.question: Defining the current state means…

screens.heading: Know the score to beat
screens.keyPoint: Document the as-is before dreaming the to-be.

screens.body: Nielsen Norman Group (nngroup.com) — the authority on user research methods, from interviews to personas. W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (w3.org/WAI) — research guidance for including users with disabilities. Usability.gov (U.S. government) — public, practical UX research method guides.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: Usability.gov has free, practical research guides.
